meta.blurb: Ravi turns thirty-five with a cake, a good job and no feeling at all. He packs a notebook and spends a month on trains, asking bakers, nuns and gardeners one question: what is joy, and how do you let it in?
meta.bible: Ravi Menon: a teacher, thirty-five, curious and a little tired; he travels by train for one month with a notebook. Dolores: an old baker in a seaside town who gives away the first warm loaves. Sonam: a Buddhist nun at a mountain monastery who teaches Mudita. Sister Agnes: a Christian nun who tends a convent garden. Mr Brandt: a retired carpenter and widower with a garden. Traditions and ideas, each correctly attributed and treated with respect: Mudita, joy in the happiness of others, one of four boundless qualities in Buddhism; Shabbat, the Jewish weekly day of rest; Rabbi Nachman of Breslov, a Hasidic teacher who lived in Eastern Europe about two hundred and fifty years ago and is remembered for teaching that joy is a great duty; the New Testament, which names joy as a fruit of the Spirit; Eid, Shukr (gratitude) and contentment in Islam; Ananda, bliss, in the Upanishads, ancient Hindu texts; Zhuangzi and Huizi, the Chinese story of the happy fish, Taoism; Seneca, a Roman Stoic who wrote that true joy is a serious matter; Diwali, Hanukkah, Christmas and Eid, festivals of light and gladness. Psychology ideas, hedged and never invented as numbers: hedonic adaptation, awe, savouring, and some studies suggesting that giving to others and singing together can lift mood. No real living people appear. Beat 50 says that if sadness stays heavy a doctor or counsellor can help; this book is general ideas, not treatment. Voice and tone: curious, warm, clear and gently funny; never preachy; joy is invited and not forced. Added for the full-length book: Meera, Ravi's friend and fellow teacher at his school. Mrs Okafor, the headteacher. Ammamma, Ravi's grandmother, who died a year before the story begins. Rachel Levin, a friend of Meera who keeps Shabbat with her family. Sister Beatrice, an elderly nun at the convent. Amina Khan, who keeps a guesthouse in a port city and celebrates Eid. Lakshmi Iyer, a temple singer. Ruth, a village choir leader. Mr Chen, a retired teacher by a river. Ms Ferreira, a librarian. Tomas, a farmer who knows the stars. Nadia, a woman afraid to enjoy a gift. Grace, a cook at a food kitchen. Mrs Odile, a volunteer of forty years. Kofi, a student who helps at a station. Mrs Petrova, who keeps a guesthouse. Marta, a farmer who rests her fields. Anton, Mr Brandt's brother. Elsa, Mr Brandt's late wife. Also named in the full-length book: Lucilius, the younger friend to whom Seneca wrote his letters; Saint Paul, whose letter in the New Testament lists joy among the fruits of the Spirit; Huizi, Zhuangzi's friend in the happy fish story; Hasidic, the Jewish movement to which followers of Nachman belong. Ravi keeps Sonam's pebble and Sister Agnes's tomato seeds, which he plants in his classroom.
chapters: A Wet Day, a Steady Heart

beats.scene: Ravi sits alone at a table with a birthday cake and a phone
beats.summary: On his thirty-fifth birthday, teacher Ravi feels flat despite having everything he wanted.

beats.scene: Ravi listens to his phone while his friend Meera speaks
beats.summary: His friend Meera phones and hears at once that something is wrong.

beats.scene: A framed portrait of an old woman stands beside Ravi's lamp
beats.summary: Ravi remembers that his grandmother died a year ago and that he has felt little since.

beats.scene: Ravi lies awake in bed while moonlight crosses the ceiling
beats.summary: Lying awake, Ravi realises he has never asked what joy actually is.

beats.scene: Ravi reads dictionary entries on a laptop at his kitchen table
beats.summary: A dictionary and a quick search give only tidy definitions, so he decides to ask real people.

beats.scene: Ravi talks with his headteacher in a bright office
beats.summary: Ravi asks for his unused holiday, and his headteacher agrees.

beats.scene: Ravi packs a small bag and a notebook beside a train timetable
beats.summary: Ravi packs light and plans a month of train journeys across the country.

beats.scene: Ravi waits on an early morning platform as a train arrives
beats.summary: At dawn Ravi catches the first train of his journey.

beats.scene: Ravi writes pleasure, happiness and joy in three columns in his notebook
beats.summary: Ravi's first notes: pleasure is quick, happiness is a mood, and joy seems deeper.

beats.scene: Ravi looks out of a train window at fields and a rising sun
beats.summary: Ravi writes his one question at the top of a page, and the countryside begins.

beats.scene: Ravi walks a seaside street at dusk toward a lit guesthouse
beats.summary: Ravi arrives in a seaside town and smells bread in the air.

beats.scene: A queue of children and neighbours waits outside a bakery at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn a queue gathers outside the bakery of an old baker named Dolores.

beats.scene: Old baker Dolores hands a warm loaf to a child
beats.summary: Dolores, an old baker, gives the first warm loaves of every morning away.

beats.scene: Ravi and Dolores stand at the counter among warm loaves
beats.summary: Ravi asks his question, and Dolores laughs and says she is only a baker.

beats.scene: Ravi kneads dough on a floured table in a warm kitchen
beats.summary: Ravi helps in the bakery kitchen, kneading dough with his hands.

beats.scene: Dolores sits on an upturned crate and tells a story to Ravi
beats.summary: Dolores explains that her mother started giving the first loaves away in a hard winter.

beats.scene: Ravi hands a warm loaf across the counter to an old fisherman
beats.summary: Ravi hands out loaves himself and feels a small, surprising glow.

beats.scene: Dolores smiles with flour on her cheek as Ravi writes in his notebook
beats.summary: Some studies suggest that giving lifts our own mood, but Dolores says she does not give for that reason.

beats.scene: Ravi and Dolores sit on the seawall at sunset sharing a loaf
beats.summary: Dolores says that bread, like many good things, is better when it is shared.

beats.scene: A small bird lands on a windowsill and then flies away
beats.summary: A bird visits Ravi's window and leaves, and he sees that joy is a visitor and not a permanent state.

beats.scene: A child tosses a broken toy aside among a pile of new presents
beats.summary: On a train a child drops a toy among a heap of new presents and asks for the next one.

beats.scene: Ravi looks at a new phone and a tidy desk in memory
beats.summary: Ravi remembers how quickly the things he once longed for stopped thrilling him.

beats.scene: Ravi writes the words hedonic adaptation in his notebook
beats.summary: Psychologists call this hedonic adaptation: we get used to good things and bad things alike.

beats.scene: A salesman in a suit shows Ravi a glossy brochure on a train
beats.summary: A salesman on the train says that he keeps buying and still wants more.

beats.scene: Ravi sits at a station café with a notebook and a blank page
beats.summary: Ravi asks whether the answer is to want less, and decides that it is not so simple.

beats.scene: A man drinks tea from a tin cup at a roadside stall
beats.summary: After a long walk, a cup of plain tea at a village stall tastes wonderful.

beats.scene: A hiker drinks water from a spring beside a mountain path
beats.summary: Ravi sees that contrast makes ordinary things vivid again.

beats.scene: Ravi sits on a train with a notebook and a small cup of coffee
beats.summary: Ravi notes that getting used to things is not a flaw, but gratitude can help us see them again.

beats.scene: Ravi walks a lane while mountains rise in the distance
beats.summary: Ravi sets out for a mountain monastery, hoping to learn about joy in others.

beats.scene: A narrow bus climbs a mountain road beside a deep valley
beats.summary: The bus reaches the end of the road, and Ravi walks the last mile to the monastery.

beats.scene: A stone monastery with prayer flags stands against a cold bright sky
beats.summary: Ravi reaches the mountain monastery, where the air is thin and cold and prayer flags flutter.

beats.scene: A Buddhist nun in maroon robes sits on a mountain terrace above the clouds
beats.summary: Ravi meets Sonam, a Buddhist nun who sits on a terrace above the clouds and laughs easily.

beats.scene: Sonam speaks while Ravi listens with a notebook open on his knee
beats.summary: Sonam says that Buddhist teachers describe four boundless qualities, one of which is joy.

beats.scene: Sonam draws the word Mudita in the dust of a stone table
beats.summary: Sonam teaches mudita, the joy we feel in the happiness of others.

beats.scene: Ravi looks away from Sonam's gentle gaze, his pencil still
beats.summary: Ravi admits that he finds it hard, because envy gets in the way.

beats.scene: Sonam and Ravi smile as a young monk shows a certificate to others
beats.summary: A young monk shows everyone his exam certificate, and Sonam is as pleased as if it were her own.

beats.scene: Sonam closes her eyes and speaks softly beside Ravi in the evening light
beats.summary: Sonam suggests a practice: quietly wish well for someone you envy.

beats.scene: Ravi sits with eyes closed, thinking of Meera under a lantern
beats.summary: Ravi tries it with Meera in mind; at first it feels stiff, then something eases.

beats.scene: Ravi writes by lamplight in a cold stone room under a thin blanket
beats.summary: Ravi writes his first lesson from Sonam: joy in others means joy is never in short supply.

beats.scene: Ravi sits at a stone table at night and lists small thanks
beats.summary: Ravi starts a list of small things he is thankful for, and Sonam smiles at the silly ones.

beats.scene: Ravi gets down from a mountain bus and boards a city train
beats.summary: Sonam gives Ravi a smooth pebble, and he travels to a city to meet Meera's friend Rachel.

beats.scene: Children set a long table while a woman stirs a busy pot
beats.summary: Rachel's family bustles through the kitchen before sunset, preparing for Shabbat.

beats.scene: A family lights two candles on a Friday evening around a laid table
beats.summary: At sunset Rachel lights two candles, and the whole flat goes quiet as Shabbat begins.

beats.scene: Rachel and Ravi sit at the table while candles burn behind them
beats.summary: Rachel explains that Shabbat is a weekly day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night.

beats.scene: A family sings around a table with wine, candles and braided bread
beats.summary: The family blesses wine and bread and sings, and the long meal begins without phones.

beats.scene: Ravi walks slowly through quiet streets on a Saturday morning
beats.summary: On Saturday Ravi feels restless at first and then slowly calm.

beats.scene: A bearded man claps and sings with friends in a small crowded room
beats.summary: Neighbours gather in a small room to sing, and Rachel's grandfather tells of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov.

beats.scene: Ravi frowns thoughtfully at the singing group with his notebook closed
beats.summary: Rabbi Nachman is remembered for saying that it is a great duty to be joyful always, which puzzles Ravi.

beats.scene: Rachel speaks gently to Ravi at the kitchen window by candlelight
beats.summary: Rachel says joy here is a practice and not a mood, and that her tradition also makes room for mourning.

beats.scene: Ravi claps and dances awkwardly in a crowded living room
beats.summary: Ravi joins the dancing and remembers a saying of Nachman about a narrow bridge and not being afraid.

beats.scene: A quiet nun waters plants in a convent garden at sunrise
beats.summary: At a hill convent at sunrise, Ravi finds Sister Agnes watering plants in the garden.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes and Ravi eat bread and honey at a wooden table
beats.summary: Sister Agnes feeds Ravi breakfast and explains the rhythm of prayer and work in the convent.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes opens a worn Bible on a garden bench beside Ravi
beats.summary: Sister Agnes explains that the New Testament names joy among the fruits of the Spirit.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes holds a ripe tomato up to the sunlight in the garden
beats.summary: Sister Agnes says that fruit cannot be forced and that a gardener only tends the soil.

beats.scene: Ravi kneels in the soil pulling weeds beside Sister Agnes
beats.summary: Ravi helps weed the garden and finds a quiet pleasure in the work.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes sits beside a sick friend in a quiet room holding her hand
beats.summary: Sister Agnes takes Ravi to visit Sister Beatrice, an old and very ill nun, and simply holds her hand.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes and Ravi sit on the garden steps in the evening
beats.summary: Afterwards Agnes says that joy and sorrow can share the same room.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes folds her hands over an old framed portrait of a boy
beats.summary: Agnes shares that she lost her brother long ago and that joy returned beside her grief and not in place of it.

beats.scene: Nuns sing evening prayers in a dim chapel as Ravi sits at the back
beats.summary: Ravi sits at the back of the chapel while the sisters sing, and Agnes says she does not ask him to believe.

beats.scene: Sister Agnes hands Ravi a paper packet of seeds at the gate
beats.summary: Agnes sends Ravi off with tomato seeds, and he writes that joy and sorrow can share a room.

beats.scene: A port city street strung with lanterns above a busy guesthouse door
beats.summary: Ravi arrives in a port city and finds a guesthouse run by Amina Khan, with the street full of lights.

beats.scene: Amina pours tea in a kitchen where children stack small cakes
beats.summary: Amina explains that Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, a month of fasting from dawn to sunset.

beats.scene: A family in new clothes walks toward a prayer ground at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn the family goes to Eid prayer in new clothes, after first giving charity to the poor.

beats.scene: Amina holds a glass of water at sunset beside an empty table
beats.summary: Amina says that the fast teaches gratitude, because after hunger a sip of water seems like a miracle.

beats.scene: A family sits at a long table at sunset sharing dates and sweets
beats.summary: Relatives gather at a long table piled with dates, sweets and rice, and the house fills with talk.

beats.scene: Children laugh as relatives press small coins into their open hands
beats.summary: Children receive small gifts of money, called eidi, and the sweets vanish in minutes.

beats.scene: Neighbours arrive at an open door carrying plates of food
beats.summary: Neighbours drop in all day, and Amina says that having an open door is part of the joy.

beats.scene: Amina smiles with her hands open in a lamplit room
beats.summary: Amina explains shukr, the Muslim idea of gratitude, and the small phrase alhamdulillah that is said all day.

beats.scene: Amina serves tea to Ravi and an old man at a quiet table
beats.summary: Amina's father recalls a saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad that true richness is richness of the soul.

beats.scene: Ravi writes in his notebook at a window above a lantern-lit street
beats.summary: Ravi notes that contentment is not the end of wanting, but the sense that what is here is already enough to enjoy.

beats.scene: A train pulls into a small temple town at dusk
beats.summary: Ravi reaches a temple town at dusk and hears a harmonium and voices from a courtyard.

beats.scene: A temple singer plays a harmonium while people sway in a circle
beats.summary: Ravi meets Lakshmi Iyer, a temple singer who leads the evening song while people sway in a circle.

beats.scene: Ravi sits cross-legged at the edge of the circle with his eyes closed
beats.summary: Ravi joins the circle, and the repeated words slowly quiet his mind.

beats.scene: Lakshmi reads an old palm-leaf book by lamplight to Ravi
beats.summary: Lakshmi explains that an ancient Upanishad speaks of ananda, joy or bliss, as the source of all beings.

beats.scene: Lakshmi draws a circle in the air with her finger on a temple step
beats.summary: For many Hindus ananda is the nature of ultimate reality and not a mood, though schools of thought differ.

beats.scene: Lakshmi laughs and points to her chest and then to her throat
beats.summary: Lakshmi says that you do not need to understand the words to sing, because the body learns.

beats.scene: People of all ages stand in rows in a village hall to sing
beats.summary: In a village hall nearby Ravi finds a choir of children and grandparents, led by a woman named Ruth.

beats.scene: A choir of mixed ages sings together in a village hall
beats.summary: Ruth says singing together seems to lift mood and bring people closer, though researchers are still studying why.

beats.scene: Ravi stands among the choir with a sheet of music and a nervous grin
beats.summary: Ravi joins the choir and sings badly, and nobody minds.

beats.scene: Ravi hums quietly on a station platform while a stranger smiles
beats.summary: The song stays in Ravi's head, and on a platform a stranger smiles back at his humming.

beats.scene: An old man feeds fish from a stone bridge over a clear river
beats.summary: In a river town Ravi meets Mr Chen, a retired teacher who feeds the fish from a stone bridge each morning.

beats.scene: Mr Chen points at the river and speaks while Ravi listens
beats.summary: Mr Chen tells the story of Zhuangzi, a Taoist thinker who lived more than two thousand years ago in China.

beats.scene: Two men on a stone bridge look down at fish
beats.summary: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi stroll on a bridge, and Zhuangzi says how happy the fish are.

beats.scene: Huizi points a finger at Zhuangzi on the bridge in a drawing
beats.summary: Huizi objects that Zhuangzi is not a fish and so cannot know what a fish feels.

beats.scene: Zhuangzi smiles and holds up a finger on the bridge in a drawing
beats.summary: Zhuangzi replies that Huizi is not him, so how does Huizi know what Zhuangzi knows?

beats.scene: Mr Chen laughs and shrugs on the bridge while Ravi smiles
beats.summary: Mr Chen says that nobody wins the argument, and perhaps the point is that some things are known only by being there.

beats.scene: Ravi sits on a river bank watching small silver fish move
beats.summary: Ravi sits by the quiet river for an hour and simply watches the fish.

beats.scene: Ravi rests a closed notebook on his knee beside shimmering water
beats.summary: Ravi feels his judging mind go quiet and notices a simple pleasure in watching with an open mind.

beats.scene: Mr Chen holds a bamboo cane beside the river and gestures at the flow
beats.summary: Mr Chen explains that Taoism values effortless action and not forcing things, as a river does not force its way.

beats.scene: Ravi writes in his notebook on the bridge as dusk gathers
beats.summary: Ravi writes that joy often arrives when we stop trying to measure it: watch first, ask later.

beats.scene: Ravi walks into a tall old library with a high painted ceiling
beats.summary: In a big city Ravi visits a library and asks the librarian, Ms Ferreira, for the oldest ideas about joy.

beats.scene: Ms Ferreira sets an old book of letters on a reading desk
beats.summary: She brings him letters by Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher who lived about two thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A Roman scholar writes a letter with a pen by lamplight
beats.summary: Ms Ferreira reads a line from one letter: true joy is a serious thing.

beats.scene: Ravi leans toward Ms Ferreira at a lamplit library table
beats.summary: Ms Ferreira explains that serious does not mean gloomy: Seneca meant a deep, steady joy that does not depend on luck.

beats.scene: A pile of sweets beside a single warm lamp
beats.summary: Pleasure depends on circumstances, but a steady joy can last through hard times, like the difference between sweets and a lamp.

beats.scene: Ravi sits in a quiet corner remembering a hospital room and laughter
beats.summary: Ravi remembers laughing with his grandmother in her last months, and sees that joy can live in a hard time.

beats.scene: Ravi and a bus driver laugh together at a joke on a busy bus
beats.summary: On the bus home the driver tells a joke, and the whole bus laughs together.

beats.scene: Passengers smile at each other as the bus drives through rain
beats.summary: Laughing together lightens the heart and puts our troubles in proportion.

beats.scene: Ms Ferreira laughs behind a desk covered in open books
beats.summary: Back at the library, Ms Ferreira tells him that Stoics enjoyed laughter too, and that seriousness and laughter are friends.

beats.scene: Ravi reads his notebook on a night train with a small lamp
beats.summary: At the halfway point Ravi reads his notes and sees patterns, and his question changes to how to let joy in.

beats.scene: Ravi climbs a dark grassy hill outside a sleeping village
beats.summary: Ravi stays in a hill village with almost no lights, and after dinner climbs the hill to look at the sky.

beats.scene: Ravi lies on a hill under a huge sky full of stars
beats.summary: Lying on the hill, Ravi sees a sky so full of stars that he cannot speak.

beats.scene: Ravi lies still with his notebook closed, small beneath the stars
beats.summary: He recalls that psychologists study awe, the feeling of being small before something vast.

beats.scene: An old farmer in a woollen hat points up at the stars
beats.summary: A farmer called Tomas finds Ravi on the hill and tells him the names his grandfather gave to the stars.

beats.scene: Two figures sit on a hilltop under the stars in silence
beats.summary: The two sit quietly for an hour; Ravi's worries seem small and he feels calm.

beats.scene: A morning bus carries Ravi through green fields toward the coast
beats.summary: Next day Ravi takes a bus to the coast, still feeling the hush of the stars.

beats.scene: Ravi stands at the shore at night with waves under the moon
beats.summary: At night on a beach, Ravi watches waves roll in under a full moon.

beats.scene: Ravi crouches at the tide line looking at foam and shells
beats.summary: Ravi sees that awe can be found in ordinary things like waves and tides if we stop and look.

beats.scene: Children run and shout through a playground sprinkler on a sunny day
beats.summary: In the morning Ravi watches children racing through a playground sprinkler and finds joy easy for them.

beats.scene: A small child pulls Ravi by the hand toward a spray of water
beats.summary: A child pulls Ravi into the game, and he gets soaked and laughs; he writes that adults forget play.

beats.scene: Commuters hurry along a crowded city pavement in the morning rush
beats.summary: In a busy city Ravi joins the morning rush and almost steps over a small flower in the pavement.

beats.scene: Ravi notices a small flower pushing through a crack in a busy pavement
beats.summary: Ravi spots a tiny yellow flower growing through a crack in the pavement and stops to look.

beats.scene: A woman in a coat stops beside Ravi to look at a flower
beats.summary: A stranger stops too, and they both look at the flower; Ravi realises joy often hides in small things.

beats.scene: Ravi stands on a city street counting small things on his fingers
beats.summary: Ravi tries an experiment: finding ten small good things on a single street.

beats.scene: A woman holds a glass of water and looks nervously at a gift
beats.summary: In a café a woman named Nadia stares at a wrapped gift and says she is afraid to open it.

beats.scene: Nadia speaks quietly to Ravi across a small café table
beats.summary: Nadia explains that when she has been happy in the past, something bad has often followed, so she braces herself.

beats.scene: Nadia gently unwraps a scarf from tissue paper in a café
beats.summary: Ravi says that bracing does not protect us; it only spoils the good moment. Nadia opens the gift: a scarf from her sister.

beats.scene: A person holds a closed umbrella in sunshine while rain falls elsewhere
beats.summary: Ravi reflects that we cannot ban sadness and keep only joy; numbing hard feelings also dulls the good ones.

beats.scene: Ravi sits on a park bench, thinking of his grandmother
beats.summary: Ravi realises that since his grandmother's death he has switched off his feelings through busyness.

beats.scene: Ravi writes in his notebook with a small, relieved smile
beats.summary: Ravi writes that he did not lose his joy but turned down the volume on everything.

beats.scene: A grey northern town with wet slate roofs and a small bus
beats.summary: Ravi travels north to a grey, rainy town and lodges in a house with a long back garden.

beats.scene: An old man with a trowel kneels beside bright flowers in a garden
beats.summary: Ravi sees an old man working in a garden full of beds and bean frames, and they talk over the fence.

beats.scene: A man with a pencil behind his ear shows Ravi his tools
beats.summary: The old man is Mr Brandt, a retired carpenter, and says he made everything in the garden except the flowers.

beats.scene: Mr Brandt sits on a bench with a mug and speaks quietly
beats.summary: Mr Brandt tells Ravi that his wife Elsa died three years ago and that he left the garden untouched for a whole summer.

beats.scene: A single bean flower opens on a tall frame in morning light
beats.summary: One morning a bean flower on the old frame made Mr Brandt come out; he knelt and started to weed.

beats.scene: Ravi and Mr Brandt dig a bed side by side in the rain
beats.summary: Ravi helps dig a bed, and as they work side by side the talk comes easily.

beats.scene: Mr Brandt holds a small framed print beside roses in evening light
beats.summary: In the evening Mr Brandt shows Ravi a photograph of Elsa, taken beside the roses she loved.

beats.scene: Mr Brandt rests his hand on a rose bush at dusk
beats.summary: Mr Brandt says that grief and joy live together in him, and he does not push away either.

beats.scene: Mr Brandt sits at his workbench staring at a letter
beats.summary: Mr Brandt mentions his brother Anton, with whom he quarrelled about their father's workshop, and says he has written a letter.

beats.scene: Two brothers shake hands at a gate after a long time apart
beats.summary: The next morning Anton comes to the gate and the brothers shake hands; Ravi notes that letting go of resentment lightens the heart.

beats.scene: Ravi reads a handwritten notice pinned to a church hall door
beats.summary: Ravi sees a notice in a city saying that a food kitchen needs volunteers, and decides to go.

beats.scene: A cook in a large apron hands Ravi an onion and a knife
beats.summary: Grace, the head cook, hands Ravi an apron and a sack of onions and tells him to start.

beats.scene: Ravi ladles soup in a busy kitchen alongside other volunteers
beats.summary: Ravi ladles soup for a long line of people, learns their names and finds a quiet joy in the work.

beats.scene: An old man smiles and nods thanks as he takes a bowl
beats.summary: An old man says thank you and Ravi notices that he is the one who feels thanked, and also shy.

beats.scene: A woman hands a coat to a stranger on a cold street corner
beats.summary: Walking home, Ravi sees a woman give her coat to a shivering stranger without any fuss.

beats.scene: Ravi writes a list of words for giving in a notebook beside a candle
beats.summary: Ravi notes that many traditions teach giving: tzedakah, zakat, dana and seva, among others.

beats.scene: Ravi rubs his tired feet at a kitchen table at midnight
beats.summary: After a night in the kitchen Ravi is tired, but the gladness stays, quiet like a hum.

beats.scene: Ravi bows his head slightly as he listens to an older woman speak
beats.summary: A volunteer of forty years, Mrs Odile, talks to Ravi, and he listens with his head slightly bowed.

beats.scene: Ravi laughs at himself while drying a heavy pan with a cloth
beats.summary: Ravi sees that he has always liked being the clever one, and that joy is easier when he does not need to be right.

beats.scene: Mrs Odile smiles with a tea towel over her shoulder at a sink
beats.summary: Mrs Odile says she stopped trying to be important and started to be useful, and that it felt like a holiday.

beats.scene: Ravi stands at a ticket desk checking pockets while a stranger offers money
beats.summary: At a station ticket desk Ravi finds that his wallet is gone.

beats.scene: A clerk behind glass shrugs sympathetically at Ravi
beats.summary: Ravi has no money and no cards, and the clerk says there is nothing she can do.

beats.scene: A young man in a rucksack hands money to a ticket clerk
beats.summary: A student named Kofi steps forward and pays for the ticket.

beats.scene: Ravi writes his address on a scrap of paper for a stranger
beats.summary: Kofi refuses to be repaid and tells Ravi to pass the kindness on to someone else.

beats.scene: A waiter holds up a brown wallet at a café counter
beats.summary: Ravi phones the café where he had breakfast, and a waiter has kept his wallet safe.

beats.scene: Ravi sits on a train writing in his notebook with a bright face
beats.summary: Ravi is moved by how much kindness strangers show, and writes that receiving is also a skill.

beats.scene: Strangers share a meal around a plain table in a small guesthouse
beats.summary: In a market town Ravi stays at Mrs Petrova's guesthouse, where strangers share one plain table at supper.

beats.scene: A lorry driver, a nurse, a student and a widow share soup
beats.summary: At the table sit a lorry driver, a nurse, a student and a widow, and the soup and bread go round.

beats.scene: People laugh around a plain table with empty bowls and a candle
beats.summary: The strangers swap stories and laughter, and nobody is important for a few hours.

beats.scene: Ravi writes by candlelight in his room above the guesthouse kitchen
beats.summary: Ravi writes that a simple meal shared with others can be a real source of joy.

beats.scene: Ravi puts a phone into a drawer and looks out at a quiet valley
beats.summary: At a farm in a green valley Ravi puts his phone in a drawer for the day.

beats.scene: Ravi sits on a farm step in silence listening to birds
beats.summary: The first hours are hard, but then he begins to hear birds, wind and people, and feels present.

beats.scene: A hammock hangs between two trees in a sunny garden with a book
beats.summary: Marta shows Ravi a hammock between two apple trees and tells him to lie in it, because she has noticed he never sits still.

beats.scene: A farm field lies empty and green beside a ploughed field

B1B2: Ravi Menon was thirty-five years old today, and he had a good job and a warm flat. He blew out the candles on his cake, and he felt strangely empty.
Meera taught at the same school, and she knew him well. She laughed and sang happy birthday, but then she asked why his voice sounded so quiet.
His grandmother, whom he had called Ammamma, had died exactly one year before. Since then he had worked hard and felt very little, and he had never really noticed it.
He lay awake and watched the light from the street move across the ceiling. It struck him that he wanted joy badly, yet he had never once asked what it was.
At breakfast he searched online and found dozens of tidy definitions. They were all correct, and none of them told him how joy actually feels.
Mrs Okafor, the headteacher, looked at him over her glasses. She said he had saved a month of holiday for three years, and that it was about time he used it.
He spread a map and a train timetable across his table and drew a loose route. It would take him to the sea, up a mountain, into the cities and then north.
The station was cold and almost empty, and a man was sweeping the floor. When the train came in, Ravi climbed aboard and felt a small flutter of excitement.
On the first train, Ravi wrote three words in his notebook. Pleasure seemed quick, happiness seemed like a mood, and joy, he guessed, was something deeper that he could not yet name.
He wrote his big question across the top of a clean page and underlined it twice. Outside the window the city fell away, and the first green fields appeared in the morning light.
The train reached the coast in the late afternoon, and the sea was a strip of silver at the end of the street. All evening a sweet, warm smell of baking floated through the guesthouse window.
Ravi followed the smell to a small bakery with a blue door. Even though it was not yet six o'clock, a line of children and neighbours was already waiting.
When the blue door opened, a small woman with white hair and flour on her arms stepped out. She was Dolores, and she gave the first warm loaves to the children without taking any money.
When the line had gone, Ravi told her about his journey and his question. Dolores laughed so hard that she had to hold the counter, and she said that she was a baker and not a philosopher.
The bakery kitchen was hot and noisy, and flour hung in the air like mist. Dolores showed him how to fold and push the dough, and soon his arms ached.
While the bread was rising, Dolores sat down and told him about her mother. In one terrible winter her mother had begun to give the first loaves to hungry neighbours, and the habit had never stopped.
On the second morning Dolores let Ravi stand at the door with the tray. When an old fisherman took a loaf from him and nodded with thanks, he felt a small warm glow in his chest.
That night he read that some studies suggest giving to others can lift our own mood. When he told Dolores, she said she gave because the bread was warm and people were hungry, not because of a study.
When the shop was closed, they sat on the sea wall with a loaf of the evening bread. Dolores broke it in two and said that nothing tastes as good eaten alone.
Back in his room, a small brown bird landed on the windowsill and looked at him. It stayed for a few seconds and flew off, and Ravi understood that joy, too, might be a visitor.
A family shared Ravi's carriage, and the little boy had a pile of new presents on his knees. He played with each one for a minute, dropped it on the floor and asked his mother for the next.
He thought of the phone he had saved for and the desk by the window that he had dreamed about at twenty-five. He had loved them for a week, and then they had simply become part of the room.

A passenger across the aisle, a retired science teacher, told him that psychologists call it hedonic adaptation. We tend to get used to good things, and to many bad things too, and our moods drift back toward their usual level.
The salesman beside him opened a glossy brochure of cars and laughed at himself. Every time he bought something shiny, he told Ravi, it took only a month before he wanted the next one.
In a station café he asked himself whether the answer was simply to want less. That sounded dull and a little sad, and he suspected it was not the whole truth.
Ravi missed his bus and had to walk five miles to the next village. The tea he drank there, from a tin cup at a roadside stall, was the best he had ever tasted.
Later a thirsty hiker on the path knelt and drank from a cold spring. She said it was the best water in the world, and Ravi smiled because he knew exactly what she meant.
In his notebook he wrote that adapting is not a fault, because it helps us cope with life. Still, he thought, we can learn to look again at what we already have.
His next stop was a monastery high in the mountains, where a friend of Dolores said a nun lived who laughed a great deal. The bus climbed slowly, and the air grew thinner and colder.
The bus stopped at a village that seemed to hang on the edge of the world. From there Ravi walked the last mile on a stony path, breathing hard and smiling.
The monastery was built of grey stone, and strings of coloured flags snapped in the wind above its gate. A young monk opened the door and led Ravi inside without asking a single question.
Sonam was a small woman in maroon robes, and she was already laughing when he found her. She sat on a stone terrace above the clouds and poured him a second cup of tea.
Ravi told her his question, and she nodded as if it were the most sensible thing in the world. In her tradition, she said, teachers speak of four boundless qualities of heart, and joy is one of them.
Mudita, she told him, is an old word that means joy in the good fortune of others. It means being glad when a friend succeeds, even if you were hoping to succeed yourself.
Ravi admitted that it sounded almost impossible for him. His friend Meera had published a children's book that spring, and he had said congratulations while feeling a sour stab of envy.
At that moment a young monk ran onto the terrace, waving a certificate from his final exam. Everyone clapped, and Ravi noticed that Sonam looked even prouder than the boy himself.
Sonam suggested a small exercise that had helped many people. He should think of someone he envied, quietly say may you be happy, and notice what his heart did.
At first the words felt stiff and silly, like a coat that was too small. After a few minutes, however, his chest loosened, and he found himself imagining Meera's real smile.
That night in a cold stone room, Ravi wrote that Sonam's teaching changes the arithmetic. If you can be glad for other people, then your supply of joy is as large as the number of people you know.
Before he slept, he also tried writing three things he felt thankful for. They were small things, such as the hot tea, the thick blanket and Sonam's loud laugh, and writing them made him feel warm.

Sonam pressed a smooth grey pebble into his hand and told him to keep it in his pocket. Then Ravi rode down the mountain and took a train to a city, where Meera's old friend Rachel had invited him for supper.
Rachel Levin's flat was full of steam, noise and the smell of soup. Her children were laying the table, and Rachel kept looking at the clock and laughing.
Just before sunset, Rachel struck a match and lit two candles. She covered her eyes for a moment, and the noisy flat suddenly became very still.
Shabbat lasts from Friday at sunset until Saturday night, Rachel told him. During that time her family does not work, shop or look at screens, and they simply stop.
Rachel's grandfather lifted a cup of wine and sang a blessing, and then the family broke a braided loaf of bread. All the phones lay in a basket by the door, and nobody missed them.
On Saturday morning Ravi felt restless and kept reaching for a phone that was not in his pocket. By noon, however, the quiet had begun to soften him, and he walked slowly through the empty streets.
That evening some neighbours squeezed into Rachel's living room, and they clapped and sang wordless tunes. Her grandfather said these songs were loved by the followers of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov.
Rabbi Nachman, the old man said, is remembered for teaching that it is a great duty to be joyful always. Ravi frowned, because he could not see how a feeling could ever be a duty.

Rachel told him that in this tradition joy is a practice more than a mood, and that singing and dancing can help it begin. She also reminded him that her people have time set aside for mourning, so grief is never forbidden.

Rachel pulled Ravi into the circle, and he clapped and stumbled and felt very silly. Her grandfather shouted a saying attributed to Nachman, that the world is a narrow bridge and the main thing is to have no fear.
Ravi took a slow train into the hills and reached the convent just after sunrise. Inside the gate a nun in a grey apron was watering rows of plants with a green can.

Sister Agnes sat him down in the kitchen with bread, honey and strong coffee. She explained that the sisters prayed together several times a day and worked in between, and that the garden was her share of the work.
When Ravi asked about joy, she opened a worn Bible on the garden bench. In a letter by Saint Paul, she said, joy is named with love and peace as a fruit of the Spirit.
Fruit is not something you can order, she told him, holding up a ripe tomato. A gardener cannot make it grow, but she can water, weed and wait, and that is what we do with joy.
She gave him gloves and a trowel and a long row of carrots to weed. The work was slow and dirty, but his mind became as quiet as the morning.

In the afternoon Sister Agnes went to visit Sister Beatrice, an old nun who was very ill. Ravi waited in the doorway and saw that Agnes said nothing wise at all, but simply sat and held her friend's hand.
Afterwards Ravi asked how she could be joyful in a room full of sorrow. Sister Agnes said that joy and sorrow are not enemies, and that they can often sit in the same room.
She told Ravi that she had lost her younger brother when she was twenty. Joy had come back to her slowly, she said, but it had come beside her grief and not instead of it.

In the evening Ravi sat at the back of the chapel while the sisters sang, and the sound made his eyes sting. Afterward Sister Agnes told him that she did not ask him to believe anything, only to look closely.

In the morning Sister Agnes gave him a paper packet of tomato seeds and told him to plant them somewhere. On the train Ravi wrote that joy is something to tend, and that sorrow need not be sent away first.
Ravi arrived in a busy port city in the evening, and the whole street was hung with little lamps. The guesthouse owner, Amina Khan, told him that everyone was getting ready for Eid.
Amina explained that Muslims fast during the month of Ramadan, eating nothing between dawn and sunset. Eid al-Fitr is the festival that comes when the month ends, and it is full of gladness.
At dawn the whole family put on new clothes and walked to the Eid prayer, with thousands of others. Before the prayer, Amina said, every family gives food or money to the poor, so nobody is left out.
Amina told Ravi that the fast had taught her gratitude. After a whole day without water, she said, the first sip at sunset feels like a small miracle.
By afternoon the house was full of aunts, uncles and cousins, and a long table was covered with dishes. There were dates, sweets, rice and a great deal of laughter.
