He sat on a wooden bench and laughed aloud, to the mild alarm of the man who had made it.

Later that afternoon he passed a hiker who had been walking since dawn and who now knelt beside a cold mountain spring and cupped the water to her mouth. She looked up with shining eyes and announced that it was the best drink of her entire life, and Ravi understood exactly what she meant. A little thirst and a little tiredness, it seemed, could polish the dull edges off ordinary things and make them gleam.

In his notebook he wrote that getting used to things is not a defect of character but a feature of the human mind, and that it probably helps us to cope with change, loss and constant novelty. Even so, he reflected, there might be ways to look again at the things we have stopped seeing, and gratitude was an obvious place to begin. Then he drew a small arrow from the word adaptation to the word attention, and he looked at it for a long while.

His next stop was a monastery high in the mountains, where a cousin of Dolores had promised him that a certain nun laughed more than anyone she had ever met. The bus climbed slowly up a ribbon of road with a sheer drop on one side, and the air grew thinner and colder with every bend. Ravi pressed his forehead to the window and watched the clouds fall away beneath him.

The bus finally shuddered to a stop in a village that seemed to hang from the very edge of the world, and the driver pointed up a stony track toward a cluster of white buildings. Ravi shouldered his bag and began the last mile on foot, gasping in the thin air and stopping every few minutes to look back over the valley. By the time the prayer flags came into view, he was out of breath and strangely light-hearted.

The monastery was built of grey stone that seemed to have grown out of the mountain itself, and strings of faded prayer flags snapped and fluttered above its gate. A young monk opened the heavy door, looked at Ravi's flushed face and gasping breath, and led him inside to a bench by a stove without asking a single question. Someone put a cup of hot tea into his hands, and he almost wept with gratitude.

He found Sonam on a stone terrace at the back of the monastery, sitting cross-legged in maroon robes with a sea of white cloud spread out below her feet. She was already laughing at something the wind had said, and she patted the stone beside her without a word of introduction. When he had caught his breath, she asked cheerfully whether he had walked all this way to ask her something silly.

Ravi explained his question and his notebook, and Sonam nodded as though it were the most sensible thing in the world. In her tradition, she told him, teachers describe four boundless qualities of the heart, which are loving-kindness, compassion, joy in the happiness of others and a calm, even balance toward everyone. The third of these, she said, is the one that most visitors forget, and also the one that most of them need.

She traced a word with her finger in the dust of the stone table, and it was Mudita, an old word from the languages in which the teachings were first recorded. It means gladness at the good fortune of other people, she explained, which is a much rarer and more difficult feeling than most of us imagine. Being sorry for someone who is suffering comes naturally, she said, but being truly happy for someone who is doing better than you is a skill that must be practised.

Ravi confessed that it sounded almost impossible to him, and he felt his cheeks grow warm as he said so. When Meera had published her first children's book that spring, he had smiled, hugged her and said congratulations, and then walked home with a small, sour stone of envy lodged under his ribs. Sonam did not look shocked in the least; she only nodded and said that envy is the shadow that follows mudita around, and that everybody has it.

At that moment a young monk burst onto the terrace waving a certificate that proved he had passed an important examination, and the other monks crowded round him, cheering. Sonam clapped louder than any of them, her whole face lit up as though the prize were her own, and Ravi realised that he was watching mudita in action. Nobody seemed to be wondering who was cleverer, and nobody seemed smaller because somebody else had grown.

Sonam then offered a small experiment, which she said had helped many people before him. He was to bring to mind someone whose success stung him, repeat silently the words may you be happy and notice honestly what happened in his chest, with no need to force a result. The point, she added, was not to feel saintly but simply to loosen the knot a little.

At first the words felt stiff and rather silly, like a borrowed coat that was far too small, and Ravi's mind wandered off to the weather and his sore legs. Then, quite unexpectedly, he pictured Meera's face on the day her book arrived, glowing and a little frightened, and something in his chest eased and warmed. It was only a small and rather shy feeling, but it was undeniably real, and he had not expected it at all.

That night, wrapped in a thin blanket in a cold stone room, Ravi wrote that mudita changes the arithmetic of happiness in a remarkable way. If a person can only rejoice in her own good luck, she can celebrate only a few times a year, but if she can rejoice in everyone's, then her supply is as large as the number of people she knows. It was an almost embarrassingly simple idea, and he could not stop thinking about it.

Before he slept, Ravi tried another of Sonam's suggestions and wrote down three small things for which he felt thankful that day. His list was modest and a little silly, consisting of a cup of hot tea, a thick blanket and the way Sonam laughed with her whole body. Yet the simple act of writing them down seemed to turn the lamp up inside him, and in the morning Sonam read the list over his shoulder and said, approvingly, that silly was a good place to begin.

When he left, Sonam pressed a smooth grey pebble into his hand and told him to keep it in his pocket as a reminder to be glad for other people. Ravi rode the swaying bus down the mountain, changed to a train and headed for a large city on the plain, where Meera's old friend Rachel Levin had written to invite him to Friday supper. He arrived at her door with dusty boots, a tired back and a head that was still full of mountain cloud.

Rachel Levin's flat was a whirl of steam, chatter and the smell of chicken soup, and her three children were racing around the table with plates and cutlery while a grandfather polished the candlesticks. Rachel kept glancing at the kitchen clock and laughing at her own haste, as though the sun were a guest who would not wait. Ravi was handed an apron and a bowl of carrots and told that guests were welcome to work.

Just before sunset, Rachel struck a match, lit two tall candles and then passed her hands slowly over the flames and covered her eyes for a moment. The frantic noise of the flat dropped away as though someone had turned down the world, and even the smallest child stood quietly with folded hands. Shabbat, Rachel whispered, which is the Jewish weekly day of rest, had just begun, and she smiled as though welcoming an old friend.

Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday until the stars appear on Saturday night, Rachel explained, and for many Jewish families it is a weekly holiday that has been kept for thousands of years. During those hours her family does not work, shop, cook or look at screens, but simply stops, as a deliberate act of trust that the world will go on without them. Ravi, whose phone had pinged twenty times that afternoon, was silent for a long moment.

Rachel's grandfather lifted a silver cup of wine and sang a blessing over it in a rich and slightly wobbling voice, and then the family blessed and tore a braided loaf of bread and passed it round the table. The phones lay silent in a basket by the door, and the soup, the stories and the arguments about nothing stretched on for nearly three hours. Somewhere in the middle of it all, Ravi noticed that he had stopped checking the time, and that he did not miss the habit at all.

On Saturday morning Ravi woke feeling restless, with his hand twitching toward a pocket that held no phone and his mind rattling with unfinished tasks. By noon, however, the quietness of the day had begun to work on him like warm water on a stiff muscle, and he found himself strolling slowly through streets with hardly any traffic. He noticed leaves, pigeons and the sound of children playing in a yard, as if somebody had cleaned a window he had never realised was dirty.

That evening a dozen neighbours squeezed into Rachel's living room, and they sang tune after tune, some with words and some with only the syllables yai-dai-dai, while a bearded man kept time with his hands against his knees. Rachel's grandfather explained that wordless melodies like these are cherished by followers of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov, a Hasidic teacher who lived in Eastern Europe about two hundred and fifty years ago. He was remembered, the old man said, as a great teacher of joy, even though his own life had been marked by illness and sorrow.

Rabbi Nachman is remembered, the old man went on, for teaching that it is a great religious duty to be joyful always, a saying that his followers still repeat to each other. Ravi frowned at this, because to him a duty was something you did and a feeling was something that happened to you, and it seemed unfair to command someone to be glad. He wrote the saying down in his notebook with a large question mark beside it, and resolved to ask somebody wiser how it could possibly work.

Rachel thought for a moment and then told him that, in her tradition, joy is understood as a practice more than a mood, something one can begin with a song, a dance or a deliberate choice to notice the good. She added, however, that the same tradition sets aside time for mourning, including the seven days of sitting shiva after a death, so that nobody is ever told to pretend. Joy and grief, she said, are both given their proper hours, and a wise person does not confuse the one for the other.

Rachel dragged Ravi into the circle, and he clapped and stumbled and trod on someone's toes and felt entirely foolish for about a minute and a half. Then the old man shouted a saying that is attributed to Nachman, that the whole world is a very narrow bridge and the great thing is not to be afraid. Ravi laughed, found that his feet had learned the steps and wrote that night that joy does not deny the fear but crosses the bridge anyway.

A slow train carried him into the green hill country, and he reached the convent at the edge of the village just as the sun cleared the ridge. Inside the old stone gate a nun in a grey apron was moving along rows of plants with a green watering can, humming quietly to herself. She was Sister Agnes, and she looked up at him as if visitors at dawn were the most natural thing in the world.

Without asking a single question, Sister Agnes sat him down at a scrubbed wooden table and fed him bread, honey from the convent's own hives and strong black coffee. Between mouthfuls she explained that the sisters pray together several times a day and spend the hours between in work, and that the garden had been her particular share of it for thirty years. Her hands were brown, strong and slightly scarred, and her eyes were very bright.

When Ravi finally asked his question, Sister Agnes carried a worn Bible out to the garden bench and turned to a letter by Saint Paul. Joy, she told him, is named there among the fruits of the Spirit, in a list that begins with love and continues with peace, patience and kindness. For Christians, she said, joy is therefore not a mood to be manufactured but something that grows in a life that is turned toward God and toward other people.

Fruit is not something you can order, Sister Agnes said, holding a ripe tomato up against the morning sun until it glowed like a lamp. A gardener cannot force a plant to grow, she explained, but she can loosen the soil, water the roots, pull the weeds and then wait with patience, and in her view the same is true of joy. Ravi wrote down the word tend in his notebook, and then he underlined it twice and put a small drawing of a watering can beside it.

She handed him a pair of old gloves, a trowel and a long row of carrots that had been quietly overrun by weeds. The task was slow, muddy and unglamorous, yet after half an hour Ravi noticed that his thoughts had stopped racing. The only sounds were the rasp of the trowel, the murmur of bees and Sister Agnes humming a hymn, and it struck him that he had not felt so peaceful since he was a boy.

In the afternoon Sister Agnes washed her hands and went to visit Sister Beatrice, who had lived in the convent for sixty years and was now very ill, and she invited Ravi to wait in the doorway. He expected cheerful speeches or comforting sayings, but Agnes offered none and simply pulled a chair close to the bed, took the old woman's hand and sat in silence. After a while Sister Beatrice smiled faintly, and the room seemed to grow lighter, as though something had been shared that could not be said.

Afterwards, sitting on the garden steps in the golden evening, Ravi asked how she could be joyful in such a sad room. Sister Agnes answered that joy and sorrow are not enemies and do not need separate houses, because they can sit side by side in the same room, like two old people who have learned to share a bench. The joy, she said, was not that Beatrice was well, but that she was not alone.

Sister Agnes then told him that she had lost her younger brother in an accident when she was twenty, and that for a long time she had believed that she would never laugh again. Joy had come back to her very slowly, she said, in small things like warm bread and the smell of rain, and it had come to sit beside her grief and not to replace it. She no longer expected the one to chase out the other, and she had found that there was room in her heart for both of them.

At dusk Ravi sat at the back of the little chapel while the sisters sang their evening prayers in long, unhurried lines that rose and settled like breathing. He was not at all sure what he believed, but the sound made his eyes prickle and his shoulders drop, and afterward Sister Agnes squeezed his arm and said that she did not ask him to believe anything. She asked only that he look closely, and she said that looking closely was a kind of prayer in itself.

In the morning Sister Agnes pressed a small paper packet of tomato seeds into his palm at the gate and told him to plant them somewhere when his journey was over. On the train that followed, Ravi wrote in his notebook that joy is something to be tended and not forced, and that sorrow does not have to be sent out of the house before joy can come in. Then he tucked the seeds beside Sonam's pebble in his pocket, where they made a small, comforting rattle.

Ravi stepped off the train in a busy port city at dusk and found the streets strung with little lamps and bright paper stars. The owner of his guesthouse, a brisk and smiling woman named Amina Khan, told him that he had arrived on the eve of Eid and that all the shops had stayed open late for the last shopping. Behind her in the narrow hall, three small children were hopping from foot to foot with excitement and waiting for the lights to be switched on.

Over a glass of sweet tea, Amina explained that Muslims fast during the month of Ramadan, taking no food or drink between dawn and sunset, and that Eid al-Fitr is the festival that celebrates the end of the month. The fast is not only about hunger, she said, but also about patience, prayer and attention to those who have little. The joy of Eid, therefore, arrives like a long-awaited friend who has finally knocked at the door, and the whole city seems to rise to greet it.

At dawn the whole family put on their best new clothes and walked through the cool streets to the open ground where the Eid prayer would be held, together with thousands of their neighbours. Before the prayer, Amina told Ravi, every family gives a gift of food or money to those in need, so that no household is left outside the celebration. Ravi watched respectfully from the edge of the crowd and was moved by the stillness of so many people bowing at once.

Amina told Ravi that the month of fasting had taught her gratitude more effectively than any lecture. After a long day without a drop of water, she said, the first sip at sunset tastes like a small miracle, and that tiny miracle had been available to her all year without her noticing. Ravi thought at once of the tea at the roadside stall and of the hiker at the spring.

By the afternoon the house was crowded with aunts, uncles, cousins and neighbours, and a long table was loaded with fragrant rice, sweet vermicelli, stuffed pastries and bowls of glossy dates. Amina pushed a plate into Ravi's hands before he could protest and informed him that guests at Eid did not stand on the edge of the room. He found himself seated between a great-uncle and a nine-year-old girl who wanted to know all about his notebook.

The elders gave each of the children a small gift of money, a custom known as eidi, and the youngest ones shrieked with delight and showed their coins to everyone who would look. Within minutes the plates of sweets had been raided and the floor was sprinkled with sugar and crumbs. Ravi noticed that even the grown-ups were glowing, as though the children's happiness were a stove that warmed the entire room.

All afternoon neighbours knocked on the door, and each of them was welcomed, fed and sent away with a covered plate for the family next door. It is the custom at Eid to visit friends and relatives, Amina said, and to forgive any quarrels that have lingered through the year. A festival, she added with a smile, is not truly complete until it has been shared with someone who would otherwise have spent the day alone.

Gratitude, which is called shukr in Arabic, is at the heart of her faith, Amina told him, and Muslims are encouraged to thank God for large blessings and for small ones alike. She often says the word alhamdulillah, which means praise and thanks be to God, and she said it as she woke, as she ate, as she finished a task and as she closed her eyes. Ravi noticed that the word worked like a bookmark, marking each good thing so that it could not slip past.

Amina's elderly father, who had been listening quietly from his armchair, quoted a saying that is attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, which holds that true richness is not having many possessions but having a rich soul. He called this quality contentment, and he said that a contented person is like a house with a warm fire that never needs to be moved. Ravi had never heard wealth described that way, and he asked for the words to be repeated slowly.

That night, at the window above the lantern-lit street, Ravi wrote that contentment is not the same as giving up on hopes or ambitions. It seemed to him more like a decision to let the present moment be enough to enjoy, even while a person goes on working toward other things. For the first time in many months, the idea did not feel like a rule, and it felt a little like relief.

A long, dusty train ride brought Ravi to a small temple town at dusk, when the air smelled of incense, marigolds and frying batter. As he walked from the station with his bag, he heard the wheeze of a harmonium and the sound of many voices rising and falling together from behind a whitewashed wall. He followed the sound across the cobbles and through a low archway, the way a moth follows a lamp.

In the lamplit courtyard a woman called Lakshmi Iyer sat on a woven mat, pumping the harmonium with one hand and singing a single line of verse in a clear, strong voice. The forty or so people sitting around her swayed gently and sang the line back, and then she sang another, so that the song passed between her and the crowd like a ball. Nobody seemed to be performing for anyone, and nobody seemed to be watching, and the whole courtyard felt like a single breathing creature.

Ravi sat cross-legged at the edge of the circle and tried at first to follow the unfamiliar words, which seemed to repeat themselves over and over in patterns he could not quite grasp. Gradually, however, the chatter inside his head slowed and then faded, until there was only breath, rhythm and the warmth of other bodies swaying close beside him. When the song ended, he realised that nearly half an hour had passed in what felt like five minutes.

Afterward Lakshmi brewed him a cup of ginger tea and told him that the Upanishads, which are ancient Hindu texts, speak often of ananda, a word that can be translated as joy or bliss. One passage, she said, declares that all beings are born from joy, live by joy and return to joy in the end. She recited a few lines in Sanskrit in a low voice, and although Ravi did not understand a word, he felt their weight.

For many Hindus, Lakshmi said, ananda is not a passing mood or a reward but the very nature of ultimate reality, something that lies beneath the surface of daily life like a deep and quiet lake. She was careful to add that the great schools of Hindu thought explain this in different ways, and that Ravi was not required to accept any of them. He appreciated the courtesy, and he wrote the idea down exactly as she had given it, without trying to decide whether it was true.

Ravi complained, with some embarrassment, that he had no idea what the words he had been murmuring actually meant. Lakshmi laughed and replied that the body understands songs long before the head does, just as a baby understands a lullaby. In this tradition, she said, singing is a way of arriving at joy and not a reward for having understood it, so he should sing now and ask his questions later.

The next day, changing trains in a small farming village, Ravi heard singing from the village hall and wandered in to listen. A choir was rehearsing under the direction of a brisk woman named Ruth, and the singers ranged in age from eight to nearly eighty, in jumpers, school uniforms and gardening boots. A teenager stood beside a retired postman, and they were sharing a single sheet of music.

During the break Ruth told him that singing in a group seems to lift people's moods and make them feel closer to one another, which many choirs believe from experience. Some studies have found something like this, she said, although researchers are still working out exactly how it happens, and it may be partly the breathing, partly the shared rhythm and partly the company. All Ruth knew was that nobody ever left her rehearsals in a worse mood than when they came.

Ruth thrust a sheet of music into his hands and stood him between a farmer with a thunderous voice and a girl of about ten who smiled at him without mercy. Ravi came in late, sang flat and lost his place twice, and yet nobody turned a head, and nobody seemed to care. By the second song he had stopped worrying about being good, and he was simply happy to be part of the sound.

The tune stayed in Ravi's head for the rest of the afternoon, and when he reached the platform he found that he was humming it aloud without having meant to. A stranger with a briefcase heard him, raised her eyebrows, smiled and hummed the next few bars right back at him. They did not say a word to each other, and yet it felt like the beginning of a conversation.

His next stop was a quiet river town built around an arched stone bridge, and every morning at about eight a retired schoolteacher named Mr Chen stood in the middle of it and scattered crumbs for the fish. Ravi had been told by the guesthouse cook that Mr Chen knew every old story in the district and would tell any of them for the price of a little company. Ravi joined the old man at the low parapet, leaned on the warm stone and wished him a good morning.

Mr Chen said that standing on this particular bridge always reminded him of a very old story from China, and he leaned on the parapet and began to tell it. It concerned a thinker named Zhuangzi, who lived more than two thousand years ago and whose writings are among the foundations of Taoism, a tradition that values simplicity, naturalness and going with the flow of things. The story, he said, was about a walk beside a river with a friend, and it was so short that it could be told in a minute.

One fine day, Mr Chen said, Zhuangzi was strolling across a bridge over a river with his friend Huizi, who was a clever man and a lover of arguments. Zhuangzi leaned over the parapet, watched the fish darting freely in the clear water and remarked that they were enjoying themselves very much. How happy the fish are, he said, as they swim about so freely, with nothing to hurry them and nowhere that they must be.

Huizi, who could never let a statement pass without examining it, at once asked how Zhuangzi could possibly know such a thing. You are not a fish, he pointed out reasonably, and therefore you cannot know what the fish enjoy. Mr Chen did a fine impression of a sceptical eyebrow, and Ravi laughed so loudly that a duck on the bank gave him a disapproving look.

Zhuangzi was not troubled in the slightest, according to the story, and he turned the question around with a gentle smile. You are not me, he replied, so how can you be sure that I do not know what the fish enjoy? The argument went back and forth a few more times, Mr Chen said, as the old friends enjoyed the sport of it.

In the end, according to the old story, Zhuangzi said that he knew the happiness of the fish simply by standing beside the river and enjoying it himself. Mr Chen added with a chuckle that nobody really wins this argument, and that perhaps the point is that some kinds of knowing cannot be reached by logic alone. They have to be felt, he said, from the inside and in the moment.

Ravi went down the stone steps to the bank and sat on a flat rock beside the water, where the current moved slowly and the small silver fish flickered in and out of the weed. For a full hour he did nothing but watch them, without writing a word or asking himself a single question. The time went by as softly as a feather falling, and when he looked up, the shadows on the water had moved a long way across it.

After a while Ravi realised that the busy commentator in his head, the one that judged and measured everything, had gone silent. In its place he felt a quiet, ordinary pleasure in simply watching, as if the fish, the weed and the sunlight on the water had made room for him among them. Whether the fish were happy, he decided, was a question for another day, and perhaps the question would not matter very much then either.

Mr Chen told him that Taoist thinkers often speak of wu wei, which can be translated as effortless action or not forcing, and which they compare to the way water behaves. A river does not shove its way to the sea, he said, but simply follows the shape of the land and arrives in good time. A person who is always straining to feel something may be doing the opposite of what the river does, and Ravi thought guiltily of all the evenings he had spent trying to feel better.

That evening, standing on the bridge as the sky turned the colour of tea, Ravi wrote a single line in his notebook, which read, watch first, ask later. It was a curious rule for a man who had set out on a journey made entirely of questions, and he suspected that it was one of the most useful he would find. Beneath him, in the darkening water, the fish went on being whatever they were, quite untroubled by anybody's questions or notebooks.

In the big city Ravi spent a rainy afternoon in a grand old library with a painted ceiling and long tables lit by green-shaded lamps. He asked the librarian, a tall woman named Ms Ferreira with half-moon glasses, for the oldest and wisest writing she knew about joy, and she raised both eyebrows as though he had asked for a map of the moon. Then she vanished among the shelves and came back with a slim, dark book.

The book contained letters by Seneca, a Roman philosopher of the Stoic school who lived about two thousand years ago, in a time of great wealth, power and danger. He had written them to a younger friend named Lucilius, giving advice on how to live well, how to face loss and how to find a steady peace within oneself. Ms Ferreira said that people had been reading them for twenty centuries and still argued with them cheerfully.

Ms Ferreira turned the thin pages to one particular letter and read a line aloud in a low and careful voice. Believe me, Seneca had written to his friend, true joy is a serious matter. Ravi burst out laughing, because he could not imagine two words that seemed to fit together less comfortably.

Ms Ferreira smiled and explained that serious, in this sense, did not mean gloomy or solemn. Seneca had meant a deep and steady joy that rests on how a person lives and thinks, she said, and not on good luck, applause or a full purse. For exactly that reason it cannot be taken away easily, and Ravi found that he had been thinking of joy as a firework while Seneca was describing a hearth.

At a corner table he drew two pictures in his notebook, one of a pile of sweets and one of a single warm lamp, and he wrote the difference beneath them. Pleasure depends on circumstances and is gone almost as quickly as it arrives, while a steadier joy is like a lamp that goes on shining even when the weather turns and the shops are shut. Both were good, he decided, but only one of them could be carried home through the dark.

Suddenly Ravi remembered his grandmother's last few months in hospital, which he had been carefully not thinking about for a year. They had played cards on her blanket and laughed helplessly at a nurse's terrible jokes, and in the middle of all that sorrow there had been something that he could only call joy. He wiped his eyes, and he understood that Seneca's lamp had been burning in that room.

On the bus back to his hotel that evening, the driver switched on his speaker and told a joke about a very lazy cow and a very impatient farmer. The whole bus erupted, including a grumpy man in the front seat who had been scowling at his newspaper since the last stop, and Ravi laughed so hard that the window fogged. For a few moments the forty strangers on board were one warm and slightly ridiculous family, riding home together through the rain.

Ravi thought about how a good laugh can make a person's troubles seem smaller for a while, as though laughter were a pair of hands that lifted a heavy bag and set it down again. Humour does not pretend that the trouble is not there, he decided, but it reminds us that we are bigger than the trouble. Shared laughter, he noticed, seemed to work best of all, because it reminded everyone present that nobody was carrying their trouble alone.

The next morning Ravi told Ms Ferreira about the bus and the lazy cow, and she laughed so loudly that a reader at a distant table hissed at her to be quiet. Seriousness and laughter are old friends, she whispered, and in her experience the people who think hardest about the great questions are very often the ones with the best sense of humour. Ravi realised that he had been treating joy as a solemn topic, and that it would probably have enjoyed the joke.

On the night train, at the halfway point of his journey, Ravi read slowly through everything he had written in his notebook. Patterns were beginning to appear, and they included giving, gratitude, attention, other people, singing and a certain kind of stillness, and each of them seemed to have turned up in more than one tradition. His big question quietly changed shape, and it was no longer simply what joy is but how a tired person might let it in.

Ravi stopped for two nights in a tiny village in the hills, where the only streetlight had broken years ago and nobody had bothered to mend it. After supper he borrowed a blanket from the landlady and climbed the grassy hill behind the church, picking his way by the faint grey of the path. Halfway up, he switched off his torch and let the dark close over him.

Ravi spread the blanket on the cold grass, lay on his back and looked up, and for a long moment he forgot to breathe. The sky was so crowded with stars that it looked like salt spilled across black velvet, and a pale river of them, which he realised was the Milky Way, poured from one horizon to the other. He had lived in a city for so long that he had forgotten the sky was this big.

He remembered reading that psychologists have begun to study a feeling called awe, which comes over us in the face of something vast that we cannot quite understand. Some research suggests that awe makes people feel smaller and yet more connected to others, and less trapped inside their own worries, although the science is still young and there is much to learn. For Ravi, lying there, the explanation seemed almost unnecessary, because he was living the experience.

Presently an old farmer named Tomas came lumbering up the hill with a lantern in one hand, in search of a missing sheep that he said had a talent for disappearing. Instead of the sheep he found Ravi, and being a hospitable man he sat down on the grass. He began to point out the stars by the names that his grandfather had used, such as the Plough, the Hen and her Chickens, and the Lamp of the Shepherd, and Ravi did not want him to stop.

They sat together for the best part of an hour, speaking only now and then, while the cold crept up through the blanket and the stars wheeled very slowly overhead. Ravi noticed that his worries, which had seemed so large and urgent in the city, now looked as small as pebbles on a beach, and that this made him feel lighter instead of lonelier. Tomas, finding his sheep at last in the church gate, went home with a satisfied sigh.

In the morning Ravi caught a rattling bus down to the coast, and he felt as though something inside him had been quietly tidied while he slept. The hedges, the farm gates and the lazy cows passed slowly by the window, and for the whole two hours he did not once reach for his phone. It was the first time in years that a journey had felt like a journey and not like a gap between two appointments.

That night he walked out to a long and empty beach and stood where the foam slid up and sank into the sand. A full moon hung low over the water, laying a wobbling path of silver from the horizon to his feet, and the waves rolled in with a soft, endless sigh that seemed older than anything he knew. He stood there until his shoes were soaked, and he did not mind at all.

Ravi realised that the same moon was pulling the sea toward him that had pulled it every night for millions of years, and that this wonderful fact was true on every ordinary evening, whether or not anyone stood to watch. He had thought that awe was reserved for mountains, monasteries and famous paintings, but a single wave, watched properly, turned out to be quite enough. The wonder had never been missing, and he had simply been walking past it.

The next morning, on a bench beside a seaside playground, Ravi watched a dozen children racing through the spray of a sprinkler, shrieking, splashing and tumbling over each other on the wet grass. Joy seemed to come to them without the slightest effort or permission, like a sneeze or a hiccup, and they gave it away as carelessly as they received it. He thought that most adults, by comparison, had learned to carry joy in a locked box.

A small girl in a yellow swimsuit marched up to the bench, seized Ravi's hand with great authority and towed him across the grass into the middle of the spray. He was drenched within seconds, his shoes squelched and his shirt clung to him, and he laughed louder than he had laughed in a year. That evening he wrote that adults lose joy by rushing and worrying, and that play was the oldest way to get it back.

His next stop was a large, noisy city, and at half past eight he found himself swept along in the morning rush with a thousand other people. Everyone hurried along the pavement with eyes fixed on a phone or on the pavement itself, and nobody looked up at the sky, the buildings or one another. Ravi, caught in the current, almost forgot that he had come on this trip to do precisely the opposite.

Then, in the corner of his eye, he noticed a tiny yellow flower that had pushed its way up through a crack in the pavement beside a lamp post. Ravi stopped so suddenly that a man behind him nearly walked into his back, and he crouched down to look at it, with the whole river of commuters parting around him. It was perhaps the size of a button, and it was entirely and stubbornly alive.

A woman in a long grey coat stopped beside him, followed his gaze and gave a small gasp of delight. She said that she had walked down this street every morning for six years and had never once noticed the flower, and for a minute the two strangers stood and admired it together. Ravi realised that joy often hides in the small things that we are too busy to see.

Ravi decided to try a small experiment and search for ten good things on a single city block. By the end of it he had found a busker playing a cheerful tune on a trumpet, a dog with truly enormous ears, a smell of cinnamon from a doorway and a window box full of red geraniums. He ran out of fingers long before he ran out of things, and he had to start again on the other hand.

In a café at the end of the street, Ravi noticed a young woman sitting very still before a small wrapped gift, with a glass of water untouched at her elbow. When he asked, with a smile, whether it was her birthday, she told him that her name was Nadia and that she was almost too afraid to open it. He asked her gently what she was afraid of, and he waited for the answer without hurrying her.

Nadia told him that the last time she had felt truly happy, at a party, she had been dismissed from her job the following week, and that ever since she had treated every good feeling as a warning sign. She braced herself against joy, she said, in the way that a person braces herself on a boat in rough weather. Ravi nodded slowly, because he recognised a part of himself in what she said, although his own version was much quieter and much better hidden.

Ravi said carefully that many people feel this way, and that although he was no expert, bracing for the worst does not seem to prevent it from arriving. It only spoils the good moment that is already here, he said, and the loss is paid twice. Nadia took a breath, slowly peeled back the tissue paper and drew out a soft red scarf, sent by her sister, with a note that said simply, for being you.

Walking away down the street, Ravi thought about how nobody is able to choose joy while banning sadness, any more than a person can keep the sunshine and abolish the rain. Some psychologists suggest that when we try to numb the hard feelings, we tend to dull the good ones along with them, and he thought that this idea deserved to be taken seriously. He drew a picture of an umbrella in his notebook, closed, with the sun shining on it.

Sitting on a park bench with his notebook open on his knee, Ravi suddenly understood something about the flatness that had followed him through the past year. After his grandmother died he had filled every hour with work so that he need not feel the sadness, and in switching it off he had unwittingly switched off the joy as well. They had, it seemed, been wired to the same circuit, and he had cut the power to both of them at once.

That night he wrote in his notebook that he had not lost his joy after all, and that he had simply turned the volume down on everything in order to survive a hard year. If that was so, he reflected, then it might be possible to turn the dial up again, slowly and gently, without being flooded by the sorrow he had been avoiding. The thought made him feel more hopeful than he had felt in many months, and he fell asleep with the notebook open on his chest.

The train carried Ravi far into the north, where the sky hung low and the slate roofs of the town glittered with rain. His landlady gave him a narrow room at the back of the house, and from the window he looked down over a fence into a long, narrow garden that belonged to an old man next door. Even under the grey sky, the garden seemed to blaze with colour, as if somebody had hidden a small summer there on purpose.

The old man was kneeling in a flower bed despite the drizzle, wearing a flat cap and a long waxed coat that had seen many winters. He had built the whole garden himself, with raised beds, a greenhouse, a bench and a row of bean frames carpentered from scraps. When Ravi waved over the fence, the old man waved his trowel in reply and shouted that the kettle was on, so Ravi went round at once.

His name was Mr Brandt, and he had been a carpenter for nearly fifty years before he retired. He walked Ravi along the paths with the proud, shy air of a man showing off his children, pointing out the beds, the bench and the bean frames. Then he declared that he had made everything in the garden except the flowers, and he added with a wink that the flowers were doing their own work.

Over tea in the greenhouse, Mr Brandt explained that the garden had always been his wife's project, and that his only part in it had been to build things for her. Elsa had died three years ago, he said, quietly and without fuss, and for the whole of the first summer afterward the beds had been left to run wild because he could not bear to go out into them. He turned his mug round and round in his large, scarred hands, and he did not look up while he said it.

One morning in the second summer, he said, he had glanced through the kitchen window and seen a single scarlet flower on one of the bean frames that he had built himself. Without quite deciding to, he had put on his boots, gone outside and begun to pull weeds, and he had been in the garden every day since. He said that it was not a cure for anything, but it was a door that had opened, and he had been walking through it ever since.

Ravi borrowed a spade and helped Mr Brandt turn over a new bed at the end of the garden, and the two men worked side by side in a companionable rhythm, lifting, turning and breaking up the clods. It is often easier to say difficult things to a person when you are both looking at something else, and for an hour the soil seemed to carry most of the weight of their conversation. The rain stopped at some point without either of them noticing, and the first thrush of the evening began to sing in the hedge.

As the evening light turned gold and the last of the rain steamed off the leaves, Mr Brandt took an old photograph from the inside pocket of his coat and held it carefully by its edges. It showed a small, laughing woman in a floppy hat, standing among the very roses that were now blooming at their feet, and the old man looked at it for a long time before he spoke. He had carried it with him every single day since the funeral, and the edges had gone soft from being touched.

Mr Brandt told Ravi that he no longer tried to push away his grief, and that he had stopped being ashamed when joy arrived uninvited in the middle of it. The two lived together in him now, he said, like old neighbours who had stopped quarrelling years ago, and on some evenings it was hard to tell which of them was making the tea. Ravi thought of Sister Agnes, and was struck by how alike their words were.

Mr Brandt also admitted, with some reluctance, that he had not spoken to his brother Anton for eleven years, because of a stupid quarrel over who should inherit their father's workshop. Last month, he said, he had been thinking about Elsa and about how short the time was, and so he had written Anton a short and clumsy letter that said only that he missed him. He had received no answer, and he was trying not to wait by the window.

The next morning a tall old man in a tweed cap appeared at the garden gate and stood there in silence for a very long moment. Mr Brandt walked slowly down the path, the two brothers shook hands as stiffly as strangers, and then, quite suddenly, they were embracing, with Anton's cap crushed between them. Ravi wrote afterward that resentment is a heavy bag, and that setting it down, however clumsily, lightens the heart.

In the next city Ravi saw a handwritten notice pinned to the door of a church hall, with a drawing of a soup ladle in the corner. It said that the community kitchen urgently needed helpers for the evening meal, and that no experience was necessary, only willing hands. He had come to ask people about joy, he thought, and here was a chance to find out something by doing instead of asking.

The head cook was a broad, cheerful woman named Grace, who looked him up and down once, handed him a blue apron and pointed at an enormous sack of onions in the corner. She told him briskly that crying was part of the service and that she did not want to see him stop until every one of them was chopped. Ravi, who had spent his life giving instructions in a classroom, found it surprisingly restful to take orders.

At six o'clock the doors opened, and a long, shuffling line of people came in out of the cold. There were workers in overalls, old men with plastic bags, a young mother with a baby and two students who looked embarrassed, and Ravi was given a ladle and a place behind the counter. Before long he was asking names, filling bowls and swapping remarks about the weather, and a quiet gladness spread through him that he could not quite account for.

An old man in a worn tweed coat took his bowl from Ravi, looked him directly in the eye and said thank you with such gentle warmth that Ravi felt his face heat up. It was a strange sensation, because he was the one who had been given something, a moment of honest connection with a stranger, and he could not tell who had received the greater gift. He murmured that it was no trouble at all, and he discovered, to his surprise, that he meant every single word of it.

Walking back to his guesthouse in the cold, Ravi saw a woman stop suddenly at a street corner in front of a shivering young man in a thin jacket. She unbuttoned her own thick coat, draped it over his shoulders, said a few quiet words and walked on without waiting for any thanks, a little taller than before. Ravi stood on the pavement for some time and thought that he had just seen joy in its shyest and most powerful form.

That night Ravi noticed that nearly every tradition he had met on his journey, in its own words and with its own customs, teaches the importance of giving. He wrote the names in a column, which were tzedakah in Judaism, zakat in Islam, dana in Buddhism, seva in the Hindu tradition and simple charity in the Christian one, and he drew a bracket around them all. Wherever he looked, he thought, people seemed to have discovered that a hand open to give is a hand open to receive joy.

After a long shift, his feet ached, his hands smelled of onions and his shirt was spattered with tomato, and yet Ravi sat at the kitchen table at midnight feeling oddly full. The gladness was not loud, bright or excited, as he had once imagined joy would be, but quiet and steady like the hum of a refrigerator in a sleeping house. He thought that perhaps most of the joy in the world was of this soft and humble variety.

On the third evening Ravi found himself washing pans beside Mrs Odile, a small and upright woman who had been volunteering at the kitchen for forty years, and who had views on everything from dishcloths to the government. She told him stories about the early days, when there had been one pot and three chairs, and Ravi listened with his head slightly bowed, as one listens to a very good teacher. It occurred to him that he had not simply listened to anyone in months.

Ravi suddenly saw that he had always liked to be the clever one in any room, the teacher, the one with the answer and the dry remark, and that this habit was quietly expensive. It was a relief to be a beginner for once, drying pans and listening, because joy seemed to come much more easily when he did not have to be right. Humility, he thought, was not so much thinking less of yourself as thinking about yourself less.

Mrs Odile told him with a twinkle that she had stopped trying to be important some forty years ago and had tried to be useful instead, and that it had felt exactly like going on holiday. Ravi wrote this down on the back of a menu, and later copied it into his notebook with a line beneath it that read, self-importance and joy do not share a room very well. He suspected that the two had never even been properly introduced, and that they would probably walk out if they were ever forced to share a table.

At a busy railway station on a Thursday morning, Ravi stepped up to the ticket desk, smiled at the clerk and reached into his jacket for his wallet. It was not there, and neither was it in his trouser pockets, his bag or the pocket of his coat, and his stomach dropped like a stone in a well. Behind him a long queue of tired travellers sighed, and somebody looked pointedly at a watch.

Ravi explained in a rising voice that he had no money, no bank cards and no other means of paying, and that he needed to reach a town three hours away that very afternoon. The clerk behind the glass was sympathetic but helpless, and the people behind him began to mutter and shuffle their feet. He had never felt so small, or so exposed, or so far from home.

At that moment a young man with a heavy rucksack stepped out of the queue, put some notes on the counter and said calmly that this should cover the ticket. His name was Kofi, he added, and he was a student, and he said it in the tone of a man mentioning the weather and not at all like someone doing a great kindness. Ravi was so surprised that for a long moment he could not find a single word to say in reply.

Ravi begged for an address so that he could repay the money, but Kofi shook his head, grinned and said that Ravi should simply pass it on to somebody else when the chance arose. Before Ravi could argue he was off, running along the platform with his rucksack bouncing, because he said he had an exam to catch and a train in two minutes. Ravi was left standing there with his ticket in his hand and his eyes, to his own surprise, wet.

That afternoon, at the next station, Ravi phoned the café where he had eaten breakfast, without much hope, and a waiter answered on the second ring. The man said that he had found a brown wallet under a table and had been wondering how to find its owner, and he promised to post it to the guesthouse in the town where Ravi was staying. Within a single day, two strangers had quietly undone the whole of his small disaster.

On the train, with his ticket tucked carefully into his notebook, Ravi wrote that most people are far kinder than the news would have us believe. He also noted that being helped is a skill of its own, because he had found it much harder to receive a gift than to give one. A person who cannot receive, he thought, may be cutting off half the traffic of joy, and he decided to pass on Kofi's kindness at the first opportunity.

In a small market town Ravi found a guesthouse run by Mrs Petrova, a stout, formidable woman with only one table, one pot and one rule, which was that everybody ate together. She served the dishes herself, in the order in which she thought guests deserved them, and she confiscated, with a stern look, any phone that appeared above the tablecloth. Nobody dared to argue, and by the end of the evening nobody wished to.

That evening the table held a lorry driver, a night nurse, a shy student and an elderly widow, none of whom had ever met before. Mrs Petrova brought a steaming pot of cabbage soup, a dark loaf and a dish of crisp pickles, and she set them down in the middle with the air of a general laying out a map. Everyone reached for the bread at once, and for a moment nobody was polite.

Slowly the conversation began to warm, and stories were swapped about long motorways, hospital nights, examinations and a hat that had once been lost in a storm. By the end of the meal the strangers were laughing like old friends, and for a few hours no one was a driver, a nurse, a student or a widow, but simply a person at a table. Ravi had rarely felt such a lively and uncomplicated gladness, and he did not want the evening to end.

That night, by the light of a single candle, Ravi wrote that a simple meal shared with other people can be a genuine source of joy, and that it does not seem to depend on fancy food. The soup had been plain and the bread ordinary, and yet the company had turned them into a feast that he would remember for years. Many of the traditions he had met, he realised, built their most joyful days around precisely this, a table and a crowd.

His next stop was a farm in a wide green valley, where a weathered woman named Marta rented out a spare room above the dairy. On the first morning, with a feeling of faint ceremony, Ravi put his phone into the dresser drawer, closed it firmly and looked out of the window at the long, quiet fields. He had never, he realised, gone a whole day without it since he bought it.

The first few hours without his phone were surprisingly uncomfortable, and his hand kept twitching toward a pocket that held nothing but a pebble and a packet of seeds. Then, very slowly, the world began to arrive, in the form of birdsong, the whisper of wind in the barley and Marta singing something tuneless as she scraped a bucket in the yard. It seemed to him that he had been living in a room with the volume turned down and had only now opened the door.

Marta led him to a faded hammock strung between two old apple trees at the end of the orchard and gestured at it with a hand like a spade. She had noticed that he never sat still for more than a few minutes, she remarked, and she ordered him to lie down, open a book and not be useful for at least an hour. Ravi, who had not rested without feeling guilty for years, obeyed with an effort.

Marta pointed across the orchard wall to a field of rough, flowering grass that nobody had sown or ploughed that year. She let one field in every few lie fallow, she explained, because land that is never allowed to rest in the end gives nothing, and the rest was as much a part of the farming as the harvest. Ravi found that he could not stop thinking about those words all afternoon, and about the way that the long grass shone in the wind.

Lying in the hammock with the leaves moving over his face, Ravi thought of the diary on his desk at home, in which every single square was filled with lessons, meetings and promises. There was no empty afternoon anywhere in it, no field left fallow, and it struck him that joy might need room in the same way that a seed needs earth. A person cannot plant anything in a space that is already full, and he had been filling his own with noise for years.

Marta's niece taught at the tiny village school at the end of the lane, and she invited Ravi, a fellow teacher, to help with the morning's reading time. He handed out an assortment of worn picture books to a crowd of excited children who had few books at home, and he sat down cross-legged among them on the dusty wooden floor. For the first time in a year, being a teacher felt like a gift and not a duty.

One shy boy in the corner had always struggled with reading, his teacher whispered, and had never once finished a sentence in front of the class. That morning, with Ravi beside him and his finger moving slowly under the words, he read a whole line aloud without a mistake, and the entire room broke into delighted cheers. The boy's face glowed like a lantern, and Ravi found that his own eyes were stinging.

Walking back along the lane between the hedges, Ravi felt that for a few hours he had been part of something much larger than his own mood or his own problems. Joy, he thought, often seems to arrive when we give ourselves to a cause, a person or a task that is bigger than we are. It has a way of slipping out of sight when we turn and stare straight at it, and this thought, rather unexpectedly, led him to the next one.

That evening Ravi sat at the little table in his room, frowning over his notebook and trying to work out an efficient method for obtaining more joy. Outside the open window a thrush was singing its heart out in the apple tree, and he did not hear a single note of it. It was a remarkably foolish thing to be doing, he later admitted, and he was the only person in the valley who did not know it.

Marta brought him a mug of tea and read his face at once, and she laughed until she had to sit down on the bed. Joy is like a shy cat, she told him, because if you chase it, it runs under the sofa, but if you get on with your life and leave the door open, it will come and sit on your lap. Ravi closed the notebook, at last heard the thrush and began to laugh as well.

Marta's neighbour had left a basket of ripe peaches on the kitchen table, and Ravi took one to the window and held it for a moment in both hands. Then he closed his eyes and ate it so slowly that the juice ran down his wrist and dripped from his elbow onto the sill, and he did not care in the least. It was, without any doubt, the best peach in the entire history of peaches, and he was prepared to defend that opinion against anyone.

Ravi remembered that psychologists call this savouring, which means pausing on purpose to let a good moment sink in and to notice how it feels in the body. Some studies suggest that people who practise it enjoy pleasant experiences more and remember them for longer, although the findings are still being tested, and it takes no more than a few seconds. It cost nothing at all, he noticed, and nobody had to give it to him, which seemed an almost suspiciously good arrangement.

All morning Ravi practised the same short pause on other small things that he would normally have swallowed whole. He stopped for a few breaths to taste his tea, to feel the first cool drops of rain on his face and to enjoy the warmth of a neighbour's loud and cheerful good morning. Each time, the moment seemed to widen a little, like a doorway opening into a larger room.

Ravi decided to begin each day at the window by writing down three small joys from the day before, in a column at the foot of a fresh page. He kept the list short on purpose, because he suspected that anything longer would become homework, and homework was the one thing that was certain to frighten joy away. Sonam's silly list from the mountain, he thought with a smile, had grown up a little, though not so much that it had lost its sense of humour.

As the days passed, his lists grew steadily more exact and also more entertaining, and the effort of finding three things began to change the way he looked at his days. One morning he wrote down warm socks, a perfectly straight line of ducks crossing a road and one really satisfying sneeze, and he laughed aloud at the sight of it. He noticed that looking for small joys seemed to make them show up more often, as if they had only been waiting to be asked.

One bright afternoon Ravi phoned Meera to tell her about a happy moment, which was a small dog on a station platform that had politely refused to leave a sandwich unattended. As he described it, the memory seemed to swell and brighten, and by the end of the call it felt twice as large as when it first happened. Joy that is told, he concluded, is joy that grows, and it was strange that nobody had taught him so.

Meera laughed warmly down the line and said that he sounded different, lighter somehow and a little silly, as though he had been left out in the sun. Ravi took a breath, told her about Sonam and about the old envy he had carried over her book, and described how he had practised wishing her well from a mountaintop. There was a long silence at the other end, and then Meera said, in a thick voice, that she had been needing to hear that for a year.

Near the end of his journey, Ravi arrived in a town on the very night of a lantern festival, and the main street was packed with people carrying lamps of red, gold, blue and green. Paper lanterns bobbed on poles, candles flickered in jars on every windowsill and children ran in zigzags, trailing sparks of glitter and laughter, so that the whole town seemed to float a little above the ground. He stood in the doorway of a shop and simply let it wash over him.

Ravi remembered that light and gladness go together in many festivals around the world, from Diwali and Hanukkah, which are both called festivals of light, to Christmas with its candles and stars and the lamp-lit streets of Eid. People in many cultures seem to have discovered the same thing, he thought, which is that the best answer to darkness is to gather together and light something. He wondered why this idea was so old and so widely shared, and he decided that perhaps the explanation was simply that it worked.

A smiling stranger lit Ravi's small paper lantern from her own, and neither of them said a word, because there was nothing that needed to be said. Back in his room he wrote a short list of what all the traditions he had met seemed to share, and it read, giving, thanks, other people, rest, song and paying attention. None of them, he noticed, required a person to be rich, clever or certain, and all of them were open to anybody tomorrow morning.

Exactly a month after he had set out, Ravi climbed the stairs to his flat, unlocked the door and set his bag down in the hall. The kitchen was precisely as he had left it, with the same table, the same chair and the same dull shelf of tidy books, and yet it looked warmer and more interesting, as though somebody had changed the light. Nothing in the room had changed, he thought, except the person who was looking at it, and that was a very large change indeed.

On Monday morning Ravi walked into his noisy classroom with his bag on his shoulder and a pebble in his pocket, and the children turned and looked up at him with wide, curious eyes. For the first time in a very long while he looked back at each of them properly, one at a time. He noticed their gap-toothed grins, their inky fingers and the girl in the front row who had grown at least two inches, and he realised that he had been teaching them for a year and had hardly seen them.

At break Mrs Okafor put her head round the door and asked him, with a quizzical smile, whether he had come back with anything interesting to say. Ravi thought for a long moment, because the whole month of trains, kitchens, mountains and hammocks pressed against his tongue, and decided that the honest answer was also the modest one. He said that he had found a great many questions, a few small practices and a better appetite for breakfast.

Ravi sat at his desk after the children had gone and had to admit that he had not found one grand, shining answer to bring home like a trophy. What he had instead was a handful of small habits, gathered like pebbles from many different tables, and he began to suspect that this was a better thing to have than a single answer. An answer can be admired from a distance, he thought, but a habit can be lived in.

Ravi took a plain white card from his drawer and wrote a short daily plan on it in large and careful letters, and then he propped it against the classroom window where he could see it. It read, notice three small joys, do one kind thing for someone else and pause for a few seconds to savour something good. It was so modest, he thought, that he might actually manage to keep it.

On the first day of his new plan he noticed something that he had somehow missed in a hundred lessons. A bar of afternoon sunlight was falling through the window and lighting up the chalk dust like a slow, silent snowfall, and every speck glowed gold as it drifted. The children below it, bent over their books, seemed to be sitting inside a small and temporary miracle, and he wrote it down at once as his first joy of the day.

At lunchtime a small boy at the front of the queue discovered that he had forgotten his money, and he stood at the counter looking miserable, with his ears turning red. Ravi stepped forward, quietly paid for the meal and said nothing at all about it, remembering the young man at the station and his two words, pass it on. The boy mumbled his thanks, and Ravi felt, as he had done at the blue door, that the glow was larger on the giving side.

Ravi placed Sonam's smooth grey pebble in the middle of his desk, where he would see it every day, and he planted Sister Agnes's tomato seeds in a pot of damp earth on the classroom windowsill. The children gathered round in a clump to watch, and a few of them asked where the seeds had come from, so he told them about a convent garden in the hills and a nun who hummed to her plants. Within a week, three small green shoots had appeared, and the whole class had named them.

A week passed, and Ravi noticed honestly that joy did not turn up every day, whatever the plan said on its card. On some mornings the three small joys came easily and the kind act was a pleasure, while on others he felt as though he were pushing against a heavy door in the wind. The plan was not a magic spell, he understood, and it was never going to be one.

That evening Ravi wrote in his notebook that joy is rather like a guest, who cannot be summoned by command but who comes back more often to a house where the door is open and the table is laid. He could not make it arrive, he noted, but he could keep the house ready and the kettle warm. The thought pleased him so much that he drew a little door in the margin and left it open.

The following week began with a grey and relentless rain, a tall pile of marking that seemed to have multiplied overnight and a headache that had arrived before breakfast. Then an email came from the office to say that the class trip to the museum, which the children had been talking about for weeks, had been cancelled for lack of a bus. Ravi read it twice, felt his stomach sink and wondered how on earth he was going to tell twenty-eight children.

When he told the class, a groan rolled round the room, a boy kicked his desk and one small girl in the front row put her head down and began to cry. Ravi felt his own temper rise, hot and sharp, and he had an urge to snap at someone, anyone, to relieve the pressure of his own disappointment. For a moment he could quite easily have done something unkind, and he knew that he would have regretted it for days.

Instead he paused, laid his hand on Sonam's smooth grey pebble and drew one slow, deliberate breath, as he had done on the mountain terrace. Then he crouched beside the crying girl's desk, told her quietly that he was disappointed as well and that it was fine to feel it. The room settled like a pond after a stone, and it was surprising how little he had needed to say.

Then he had an idea, and he asked the class to build the museum that they had been promised out of paper, cardboard, glue and imagination. By the afternoon the room was filled with paper dinosaurs, a cardboard mummy and a great many sticky fingers, and the mood had changed completely, though the rain outside had not let up for a moment. It was not the trip they wanted, but it was something they made together.

That evening a heavy sadness settled over him without any clear reason, and the face of his grandmother rose up in his mind with her dry, kind smile. Instead of rushing to fill the silence with noise, as he would have done a month earlier, he made a mug of tea and sat with the feeling, thinking of Mr Brandt and his two old neighbours, grief and joy. A few tears ran down his face, and he let them fall without wiping them away, and they felt strangely clean.

After a while he noticed that something else had quietly come to sit beside the sadness, and it was a small, steady gladness that he had loved his grandmother so well. The sorrow, he understood, was simply the other face of the love, and neither of them was a sign that anything was wrong with him. He felt as though two old friends who had been avoiding each other for a year had finally been introduced, and they were getting on well.

The next morning, with the rain gone and the pavements steaming, Ravi wrote a deliberately terrible joke on the board before the lesson began, about a mathematician who was afraid of negative numbers. The students groaned loudly and then began to laugh, first one, then five, then the whole room, until even the girl who had wept the day before was wiping her eyes. The laughter lifted him up and carried him along with it, and he thought that he had never been so glad to be laughed at.

In the middle of the laughter, Ravi felt a wave of deep gladness rise in him, the kind he had been missing for a very long time, and he knew at once what it was. He stopped for a few seconds, as he had learned to do with the peach, and let the feeling sink in all the way down while the room rang around him. It was not a firework, he thought, but a hearth, and it was already warm.

Later in the week Ravi told the class the story of Zhuangzi, Huizi and the happy fish, drawing the bridge and the river on the board in blue chalk. The children argued about it so eagerly, some saying that you cannot know a fish's mind and others that you can see it in the way it swims, that the bell rang twice before anyone noticed. One boy said that the real question was whether the fish knew that Zhuangzi was watching.

At the end of the day one of the girls turned in the doorway and told Ravi, with the frankness of the very young, that he seemed to smile a lot more than he used to. That evening he sat down at the kitchen table and wrote postcards of thanks to Dolores, Sonam, Sister Agnes, Rachel, Amina and Mr Brandt. He wrote to all the other people who had given him an hour, a meal or a sentence, and it took him until midnight, and he enjoyed every word.

Within two weeks the replies began to arrive, and Ravi opened each one slowly at the kitchen table, as one opens a present. Dolores sent a recipe for her morning bread, with a scrawled warning about too much salt. Sonam sent a single line of kind words in careful handwriting, and Mr Brandt wrote that Anton had come to tea twice and was already arguing about the bean frames, and Ravi read every one of them three times over.

On Sunday morning Ravi rolled up his sleeves, put on his blue apron and followed Dolores's recipe line by line, kneading the dough on the kitchen table with the heel of his hand. The first loaf came out rather flat and the second a little burnt, but the smell that filled the flat was so warm and sweet that he stood in the kitchen with his eyes closed. It was the smell of a seaside town at dawn, and for a moment he could almost hear the gulls and the blue door opening.

Then he wrapped the best of the loaves in clean cloths and knocked on the doors of his neighbours, the elderly woman downstairs, the young couple with the baby and the man who always seemed to be in a hurry. He gave the first warm loaves away without asking for anything, just as Dolores did, and the faces that appeared at each door were surprised, then puzzled, then very pleased. By the time he climbed the stairs again, he had only one crust left for himself, and he ate it standing at the window, perfectly content.

That night Ravi sat down to write his own definition of joy at last, the answer to the question that he had written across the top of a page on the first train. His first attempts were too long, too clever and rather pleased with themselves, and he crossed them out one after another until the page looked like a battlefield. He remembered Mrs Odile, and the wisdom of being useful instead of important, and he began again with a much shorter pencil and a much lighter heart.

At last he wrote something simple, and he looked at it for a long time before he was satisfied. Joy, it said, is a quiet gladness at being alive and connected to other people, and it is available, in a small way, even in hard times. It is not the same as pleasure, he added underneath, because it can sit beside sorrow, and it is not the same as happiness, because it does not depend on how the day goes.

The next day Ravi read his definition aloud to Meera over a cup of terrible staffroom coffee, feeling more nervous than any exam had ever made him. She listened carefully, said that it was good, and then added that he should include a line to say that joy is not a duty, because tired people do not need yet another thing to fail at. He saw at once that she was right, and he added the line in the margin before his coffee had even gone cold.

Ravi turned back to the page where he had written Rabbi Nachman's saying that it is a great duty to be joyful, with the large question mark still beside it. Perhaps, he thought, the duty was not to feel joyful every minute, which nobody could manage, but to keep the door open and to refuse to bolt it against the gladness that might pass by. He did not know whether the old teacher would have agreed, and he wrote that down as well.

Ravi reminded himself, as he read through his notes, that he was a teacher with a notebook and not an expert on the human mind. He knew that for some people sadness is a real illness, and that it needs proper care from a doctor or counsellor, not merely a list of small joys or a good piece of advice. What he had gathered were ideas from many traditions, and they were offered as company on the road, and never as a cure.

Early one Sunday morning Ravi took a long walk along the road that led out of town and into the fields. The sun was just lifting itself over the horizon, pouring a warm gold light down the road ahead of him, and he walked toward it slowly with his hands in his pockets and the pebble warm in his fist. He did not feel excited or triumphant, but only quietly and steadily glad, and he thought that this was quite enough for one morning.

Joy cannot be forced or bought or kept, but it can be invited, and Ravi believed that small daily habits are the way to make it feel welcome. This book offers general ideas only, and if sadness stays heavy for weeks, or you ever feel unsafe, please speak to a doctor, a counsellor or someone you trust. For everyone else, the invitation is simple, and it begins with whatever small good thing is in front of you today.
